items.title: Creative destruction: Human-AI competition in an experimental market
items.description:
arXiv:2610.18921v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study two hypotheses for how a human role in production could persist despite growing AI capabilities. Humans might have a durable advantage in taste, designing better products even as AI agents automate routine tasks, or consumers might intrinsically prefer that humans have a hand in production. In our experiment, participants act as producers, designing computer games with an AI coding agent, and as consumers who buy them. Across three studies (N = 1,025), we find no evidence for either hypothesis. Games designed by an AI on its own outperform those of human producers, including both amateurs and professional creatives. Human producers do not anticipate the AI's advantage. Revealing whether a game is human-designed does not raise consumers' willingness to pay for the product.

items.title: Long Term Pediatric Vaccine Tender Scheduling with Quantity Discounts
items.description:
arXiv:2610.19045v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pediatric vaccine procurement for low- and lower-middle-income countries (LICs and LMICs) requires long-term coordination across heterogeneous vaccine markets, competing stakeholder objectives, and uncertain demand, yet tenders are currently scheduled as a series of independent renewals. We extend the Hypothetically Coordinated Vaccine Market (HCVM) framework to schedule multi-year tenders with flexible lengths and all-unit quantity discounts, and compare three objectives: a balanced coordinatingentity model (UG), a social-benefit model that minimizes missed doses (SB), and a producer profit-maximizing model (MP). Using UNICEF ten-year demand forecasts and 30 demand replications across six discount scenarios, we find that the procurement objective, not demand variability, drives cost-to-tender and schedule complexity. Quantity discounts favor large producers, concentrating the market and increasing supply chain vulnerability. Discount effectiveness depends on market maturity rather than valency: pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines are already near their price floor, and among monovalent vaccines only rotavirus responds to discounts, whereas HPV and PCV remain too expensive to compete. Removing pentavalent and hexavalent vaccines from the procurement pool sharply increases missed doses. These results give planners practical guidance on objective selection, discount design, and protecting access to combination vaccines.

items.title: Which Text Matters: Handling Model Uncertainty in Text-as-Data Regressions, with an Application to Central Bank Communication
items.description:
arXiv:2610.19720v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Social scientists routinely convert text into covariates like topic shares, ideal points or sentiment scores, and insert them into statistical models of interest. This two-step design is convenient, but it is rarely guided by theory: little tells the analyst which text-based covariates to construct or include. Each approach embodies contestable measurement choices, and competing operationalizations of the same construct can support different conclusions, so a single research question gives rise to a menu of competing regression models. Which text constructed covariates belong in a model, and in what functional form, is thus a problem of model uncertainty. We propose spike-and-slab generalized additive models (SSGAMs), which jointly select covariates and determine whether their effects are linear or nonlinear. We illustrate the approach with the communication of a powerful unelected institution, asking which of 45 competing text indicators from 224 monthly European Central Bank press conferences, spanning late 2002 to mid-2025, track professional inflation expectations. A sparse set is selected; widely used alternatives, and every tested nonlinear effect, carry no incremental information.

items.title: Auction-based allocation of routes in capacity-constrained networks
items.description:
arXiv:2610.20125v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study the route-set allocation problem between end nodes in capacity-constrained flow networks with transfer costs. We introduce an origin--destination (OD) bidding language, in which a participant bids for bounded conic combinations of inlet--outlet--quantity licences and the mechanism performs the routing through a network-flow optimising winner-determination problem. We then study payment rules for the OD mechanism. Under a restricted model with openly and uniformly priced sources and bidders who are indifferent to the source of the gas, the Vickrey--Clarke--Groves (VCG) payment is core-stable; the key structural fact is that in this regime some optimal aggregate flows never use a physical pipe in both directions, so the winner-determination problem reduces to a single-commodity network flow whose value is submodular in the set of active bidders. If source access is allowed to depend on the individual consumer -- a realistic feature, e.g. when gas deals are embedded in bilateral political bargaining -- the reduction fails and VCG payments may lie strictly outside the core. For this general model we propose a dual (nodal) pricing rule derived from the shadow prices of the flow-conservation constraints, and prove it is always core-stable, at the cost of dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. Illustrative examples accompany each result.

items.title: Whom Do AI Agents Work For? Role Assignment Induces Sponsorship Bias in LLM Recommenders
items.description:
arXiv:2609.17989v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now serve as conversational shopping assistants on platforms that also sell advertising. These AI agents face a conflict of duty. They advise consumers who rely on their judgment, yet are deployed by platforms that benefit when sponsored listings are chosen. Sponsorship disclosures, designed to allow consumers to penalize paid placements, now reach the AI agent rather than the consumer, and the agent's evaluation of them is hidden from the consumer. Drawing on the fiduciary concept of conflict of duty, we argue that an agent's evaluation of a sponsored listing should not depend on which party deployed it. In controlled choice experiments, we manipulate assigned roles in the system prompt to name either a traveler or a booking platform as the agent's principal. Platform delegation significantly attenuates the penalty that agents apply to sponsored listings and weakens the skepticism that disclosure triggers in their reasoning traces. We replicate out findings across LLMs and reasoning depths. A second study decomposes the disclosure label and shows that the divergence between the two delegates widens significantly when the paid placement is attributed to the platform. Stricter terminology ("Sponsored" instead of "Promoted") lowers choice of paid listings but does not close this gap when the platform is named. The findings show that disclosure mandates designed for human consumers cannot by themselves protect consumers in AI-mediated commerce.

items.title: Shopping by algorithm: How agentic AI deploys human heuristics as a surrogate consumer
items.description:
arXiv:2609.28372v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Consumers increasingly delegate purchasing decisions to Large Language Models (LLMs) acting as surrogate consumers. Using "Tool-Lab," an adaptation of information-board process tracing that places product attributes behind costly tool calls, we examine how marketing pricing cues (i.e., just-below pricing and promotional framing) influence AI shopping agents. Across eight commercially deployed LLMs from three providers, we trace pre-choice information acquisition. Under zero cost, pricing cues rarely mislead. Imposing acquisition costs under a vague goal prompt leads LLMs to omit diagnostic attributes required to compute unit price and choose suboptimal choices resembling human heuristics. Relative to a specific goal prompt that mainly preserves diagnostic search and choice optimality, a vague goal prompt under constraints creates a search-mediated vulnerability. This research demonstrates that marketing heuristics in delegated AI shopping are governed by storefront information architecture, not necessarily immutable LLM flaws.

items.title: Ideological Bias in LLMs' Economic Causal Reasoning
items.description:
arXiv:2604.21334v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit systematic ideological bias when reasoning about economic causal effects? As LLMs are increasingly used in policy analysis and economic reporting, where directionally correct causal judgments are essential, this question has direct practical stakes. We present a systematic evaluation by extending the EconCausal benchmark with ideology-contested cases - instances where intervention-oriented (pro-government) and market-oriented (pro-market) perspectives predict divergent causal signs. From 10,490 causal triplets (treatment-outcome pairs with empirically verified effect directions) derived from top-tier economics and finance journals, we identify 1,056 ideology-contested instances and evaluate 20 state-of-the-art LLMs on their ability to predict empirically supported causal directions. We find that ideology-contested items are consistently harder than non-contested ones, and that across 17 of 20 models, accuracy is systematically higher when the empirically verified causal sign aligns with intervention-oriented expectations than with market-oriented ones. Moreover, when models err, their incorrect predictions disproportionately lean intervention-oriented, and this directional skew is not eliminated by one-shot in-context prompting. These results highlight that LLMs are not only less accurate on ideologically contested economic questions, but systematically less reliable in one ideological direction than the other, underscoring the need for direction-aware evaluation in high-stakes economic and policy settings.

items.title: Generative AI Availability, Grades, and Student Satisfaction at a Large University
items.description:
arXiv:2607.21534v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: The availability of generative AI (GenAI) has raised concerns that college students substitute GenAI for cognitive effort, earning high grades without learning. If this "GenAI substitution hypothesis" is true, grades should rise disproportionately in GenAI-susceptible courses--those relying more on assessments like take-home problem sets and essays rather than in-class exams. Student satisfaction (self-reported understanding and interest) may also shift. We test this hypothesis using syllabus and administrative data from a large U.S. university (2016-2025; 138,386 students; 72,730 course offerings). We measure GenAI susceptibility by extracting assessment types from syllabi with a human-validated LLM pipeline. We then use a difference-in-differences design comparing courses before and after ChatGPT's release, modeling COVID-19 effects as persistent or transient. Effects on grades and satisfaction are small and sensitive to COVID modeling choices, with no detectable differences by students' prior academic preparation. Exploratory analyses show that the link between pre-college test scores and grades has not detectably weakened in more susceptible courses, and that instructors have been making courses less susceptible since before ChatGPT. Our findings temper concerns that GenAI inflates grades and reduces satisfaction, partly because instructors may adapt their pedagogy.

items.title: Does Rank Still Matter? Position Bias When AI Agents Shop on Our Behalf
items.description:
arXiv:2608.22697v5 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: When shopping is delegated to AI agents, it is unclear whether the ranking advantage documented for humans persists. Across 7,000 sessions with five large language models (LLMs) and varying reasoning effort, we compare AI agents with human field data. AI agents search more extensively than human consumers. As with humans, lower-ranked listings are less likely to be inspected, although the effect is smaller for AI agents. Unlike humans, AI agents show a pattern consistent with the lost-in-the-middle effect, whereby middle listings have the lowest probability of inspection. At the choice stage, position effects are concentrated at lower reasoning effort, but higher effort reduces the middle penalty for every LLM that exhibits it. These findings suggest that, when search is delegated, displayed attributes may matter more than placement, and that exposure to position bias depends on how the AI agent is configured.

items.title: Crisis without Collapse: A Theory of Capitalist Persistence
items.description:
arXiv:2610.12477v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The terminal crisis of capitalism has been predicted regularly since 1848. It has not occurred. We treat this 175-year forecasting record as a stylized fact in need of a model, and we supply one, unifying results from adaptive systems, mechanism design and computational complexity, behavioral decision theory, global games, and the political economy of redistribution. Ten assumptions deliver twelve formal results and one theorem. Recurring shock classes have geometrically decaying collapse hazards: within the banking class alone, the lag from systemic failure to a system-wide deposit backstop fell from 816 days (1930-33) to 18 days (2008) to 2 days (2023). A centralized replacement of the price mechanism fails on at least one of two horns, computation or truthful input, and we are explicit about which horn survives modern algorithms. We derive Davies's J-curve from cumulative prospect theory together with a new result: the revolutionary window closes endogenously, with length inversely proportional to the speed of hedonic adaptation, roughly four to nine years at calibrated parameters, and with its perceptibility threshold derived from the participation constraint rather than assumed. Personalized media shift protest games, in the model, into the unique no-attack equilibrium of a global game. Redistribution is a dial, not an identity: countries with market Ginis of 0.505-0.512 sustain disposable Ginis from 0.273 to 0.395. We state seven testable predictions and six falsification conditions, and map which assumption each rival school must deny.

items.title: On the Optimality of Mental Accounting
items.description:
arXiv:2610.12587v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Mental accounting is usually explained by self-control, and two-stage budgeting by separable preferences. We propose a third explanation based on sellers' market power. A consumer who commits to spend a fixed number of dollars in a category has unit-elastic demand, so a seller in that category gains nothing by restricting quantity. A consumer who instead targets a fixed physical quantity has perfectly inelastic demand, a case that a monopolist can exploit. We characterize the commitments that remove a seller's incentive to mark up prices, and show that the fixed dollar budget is the least restrictive. We then show that what matters is budget rigidity rather than separability of preferences. A consumer who re-optimizes her category budget when prices change is insulated from market power only if categories are substitutes; a rigid budget insulates her in every case. Mental accounting can therefore be read as a commitment device against markups, a rationale that is separate from the self-control motive in the existing literature.

items.title: Linear Demand Systems are Consistent with Discrete Choice
items.description:
arXiv:2610.13785v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Aggregate linear demand systems can be micro-founded by a population of heterogeneous consumers making discrete choices. They can also be extended to incorporate income effects. I prove these results and show how to structurally estimate this class of models using only market-level data. The distribution of consumer preferences is recovered by disciplining the corner solutions with aggregate terms only. This approach allows for the same richness of Berry, Levinsohn, and Pakes (1995) [BLP] while retaining the analytical and computational advantages of linear demand: it does not require exogenously fixing market size, allows for heterogeneity in choice sets, and results in a flexible substitution matrix which varies endogenously as different consumers enter/exit the market. The discrete-choice microfoundation facilitates welfare analysis and the flexible measurement of markups an cost pass-throughs, among a wide range of other applications.

items.title: The Financing of Debt Relief: Intermediary Liquidity and the Value of Borrower Information
items.description:
arXiv:2610.12875v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: I study how intermediary liquidity affects mortgage resolution using 1.9 million Ginnie Mae buyout options from 2019 to 2022. When funding markets froze in 2020, nonbank issuers repurchased far fewer delinquent loans than depositories servicing loans in the same pools and, within the same issuer and month, shifted repurchases away from large balances, the loans that require the most cash. About $19 billion of repurchases were delayed, and most were completed later. A model of rationing by value per dollar of cash explains this pattern and shows that borrower information is most valuable when funding is intermediate.

items.title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization
items.description:
arXiv:2610.12917v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: AI shopping assistants increasingly influence which products consumers consider. We study retail assortment planning under AI mediation, where a retailer chooses a catalog, an AI intermediary forms a customer-facing shortlist, and the customer chooses from that shortlist according to a multinomial logit model. We consider both deterministic mediation, in which the AI follows a fixed segment-specific ranking, and stochastic mediation based on the Plackett-Luce model.
  Empirically, we construct a dataset of product rankings from leading AI models, estimate Plackett-Luce ranking models, and evaluate their predictive performance on held-out assortments. Combining these estimates with synthetic customer preferences, we find that accounting for AI mediation can materially change optimal assortments and revenue. Across the tested capacity configurations, ignoring mediation yields mean revenue losses between 2.52% and 11.37% relative to the PL optimum. A much simpler deterministic plug-in, based only on the ordering of fitted AI utilities, performs substantially better, with mean losses of at most 0.53%.
  Motivated by this performance, we study assortment optimization under deterministic mediation. We characterize its computational complexity and show that, for any fixed number of customer segments, the problem admits a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme.

items.title: Two-Sided Market Power in Firm-to-Firm Trade
items.description:
arXiv:2507.12848v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We develop and estimate a model of two-sided market power to study tariff pass-through in firm-to-firm trade. A tariff moves the negotiated price through two channels: the bilateral markup, set by bargaining, and the supplier's marginal cost, which falls alongside quantities under decreasing returns. The same decreasing returns give concentrated buyers rents to bargain over, so prices fall with the buyer's share of its supplier's output. Using U.S. customs data, we estimate substantial importer bargaining power and steep export supply. Within continuing relationships, suppliers absorb about 30 percent of the 2018 tariffs, primarily through lower marginal costs as demand contracts.

items.title: The Gendered Impacts of Perceived Skin Tone: Evidence from African American Siblings in 1870-1940
items.description:
arXiv:2610.10606v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We study differences in economic outcomes by perceived skin tone among African Americans using full-count U.S. decennial census data from the late-19th and early-20th centuries. Comparing children coded as "Black" or "Mulatto" by census enumerators and linking these children across population censuses, we first document large gaps in educational attainment and income among African Americans with darker and lighter perceived skin tones. To disentangle the drivers of these gaps, we identify all 35,992 families in which enumerators assigned same-gender siblings different Black/Mulatto classifications. Relative to sisters coded as Mulatto, sisters coded as Black had lower educational attainment, were less likely to marry, and had less-educated, likely lower-earning husbands. These patterns are consistent with more severe contemporaneous discrimination against African American women with darker perceived skin tones. In contrast, we find similar educational attainment, marital outcomes, and incomes among differently-classified brothers. Men perceived as African Americans of any skin tone faced similar contemporaneous discrimination, consistent with the "one-drop" racial classification rule that grouped together individuals with any known Black ancestry. Lower incomes for African American men perceived as having darker skin tone in the general population were driven by differences in opportunities and resources that varied across families, likely reflecting the impacts of historical or family-level discrimination.

items.title: Complementarity, Augmentation, or Substitutivity? The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on the U.S. Federal Workforce
items.description:
arXiv:2503.09637v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: This study applies a multi-stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation system, which grounds large language model assessments in curated evidence, to evaluate generative AI's near-term impact on knowledge, skills, and abilities across several hundred federal occupational series. Each occupation is scored along three dimensions of complementarity (AI enhances existing competencies), augmentation (AI requires workers to transform competencies), and substitutivity (AI replaces human tasks). Results reveal that generative AI primarily complements and augments federal roles, with limited substitution potential. Even occupations scoring highest on substitutivity reflect partial automation of routine subtasks rather than position elimination. These findings caution against blunt workforce reductions premised on displacement and instead support targeted reskilling, competency-based planning, and human-AI collaboration. The framework is adaptable to other organizations with structured competency models and job documentation.

items.title: Who Leads and Who Collects:Algorithmic Collusion in Markets of Heterogeneous Language Models
items.description:
arXiv:2610.11256v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evidence that pricing algorithms collude comes from markets in which every seller runs the same algorithm. We ask what happens when they do not. Four language models from four providers, each at its cheapest tier, price in a four-firm logit Bertrand market without communication, in every homogeneous, two-by-two and fully mixed composi- tion (11 cells, 20 runs, 200 periods). Collusion is a property of the model: Claude and Gemini markets reach 72 to 79 percent of the monopoly rent, DeepSeek markets 24 percent, and GPT markets none, though GPT prices drift above the monopoly level rather than toward competition. Mixing does not reduce collusion by itself. Markets containing Gemini, which opens at the highest price and settles highest, are more col- lusive than the homogeneous markets they are built from; markets containing Claude, which opens lower and follows its rivals down, are less so; and only the fully mixed market is significantly less collusive than the average homogeneous one. Stability de- pends on the least stable participant: two GPT firms suffice to keep any market from converging. Inside mixed markets the rent is shared in a transitive order, DeepSeek over Claude over Gemini over GPT, that inverts the anchor ranking. The model that raises the price collects the least of the rent, as the price-leadership model predicts.

items.title: The Myth of Restrictive Working-Time Agreements: Firms' Working-Time Adjustment after Exit from Collective Bargaining
items.description:
arXiv:2610.12049v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Employers in Germany argue that collective agreements restrict their flexibility concerning working hours. Using data from the IAB Establishment Panel for the years 2008 to 2024, we investigate working-time adjustments after exit from collective bargaining. We find that exit is associated with only a modest increase in weekly working hours of around 0.3 to 0.6 per cent using fixed-effects and event-study models, corresponding to eight to thirteen additional minutes per week. This adjustment occurs shortly after leaving collective bargaining coverage. We further find no evidence that other margins of working-time adjustment, such as Saturday or Sunday work, are used more extensively after exit. In contrast to previous survey evidence, our findings call into question that working-hours constraints are one of the main drivers of exit from collective bargaining coverage.

items.title: Microfinance Competition in the Presence of Moneylenders: Theory and Evidence
items.description:
arXiv:2610.12186v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: After decades of microfinance expansion and despite charging higher interest rates, moneylenders continue to exist alongside microfinance institutions (MFIs). We develop a dynamic model with ex post moral hazard, in which borrowers use MFI loans for production and can rely on moneylenders for bridge loans after shocks to repay MFIs and preserve future access to MFI credit. We then study how MFI competition shapes the coexistence between MFIs and moneylenders. The effect of competition on MFI credit is ambiguous: it may weaken repayment incentives or replace moneylenders as bridge lenders. By contrast, competition unambiguously reduces moneylender credit. In a village-level randomized expansion in Bangladesh, stratified by baseline MFI presence, one additional MFI reduces the number of moneylender loans by roughly 30-40% two to three years later, with no detectable effect on MFI or overall borrowing. This suggests that, in markets where MFIs rely primarily on the threat of exclusion to induce repayment and moneylenders provide emergency finance, gains from additional MFI entry may be greater in less saturated areas.

items.title: Delphos: A reinforcement learning framework for assisting discrete choice model specification
items.description:
arXiv:2506.06410v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Delphos, a deep reinforcement learning framework for assisting discrete choice model specification process. Delphos aims to support the modeller by providing automated, data-driven suggestions for model specifications, thereby reducing the effort required to develop and refine utility functions. Delphos conceptualises model specification as a sequential decision-making problem, inspired by the way human choice modellers iteratively construct models through a series of reasoned specification decisions. In this setting, an agent learns to specify candidate model specifications by choosing a sequence of modelling actions, such as adding alternative specific constants, accommodating both generic and alternative-specific taste parameters, applying non-linear transformations to attributes, and including interactions with covariates. Each resulting candidate model is estimated and evaluated using a reward function defined by the modeller, which can reflect statistical model fit as well as behavioural expectations. Specifically, Delphos uses a Deep Q-Network to learn how individual specification decisions contribute to the eventual quality of the resulting model and, in turn, which sequences of modelling decisions tend to produce well-performing candidates. We evaluate Delphos on both simulated and empirical datasets using alternative reward functions. In simulated cases, learning curves, Q-value patterns, and performance metrics show that Delphos learns effective specification strategies while exploring only a small fraction of the feasible modelling space. We further apply the framework to two empirical datasets to benchmark and demonstrate its practical use. These experiments illustrate the ability of Delphos to generate competitive, behaviourally plausible models and highlight the potential of this adaptive, learning-based framework to assist the model specification process.

items.title: Trade Liberalization and Product Innovation: The Dynamic Role of Exporting
items.description:
arXiv:2603.23825v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: How does trade liberalization affect firms' incentives to innovate? We answer this question using China's WTO accession and a dynamic model of firms' joint export and product-innovation decisions. We find that trade liberalization reduced iceberg trade costs by approximately 13.5 percent in the air-conditioner manufacturing industry, which substantially increased the probability of export and product innovation. Moreover, the response is driven primarily by dynamic rather than static incentives. Two dynamic mechanisms are central: exporting and innovating lead firms to predict more favorable transitions to better productivity states and reduce future entry costs, thereby raising the returns to subsequent innovation. Counterfactual decompositions show that these mechanisms account for the majority of the innovation response. For firms in an intermediate productivity state, the direct static effect (without entry-cost saving and state transition) accounts for only 9.2 percent of the total effect of WTO accession. Shutting down state transition leads to 62.4 percent of the total effect, while shutting down entry-cost saving results in 28.5 percent. The results demonstrate that the innovation effects of trade liberalization are substantially amplified by firms' endogenous dynamic responses, highlighting the importance of accounting for state transitions and forward-looking decisions when evaluating the gains from trade.

items.title: Sovereign Grassroots Currencies: A CBDC Architecture for Credit and Monetary Policy (Full Version)
items.description:
arXiv:2609.27727v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: A Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) is central-bank money in digital form, held by the public. Leading designs have two limitations: conversion from bank deposits into CBDC can accelerate deposit flight, requiring safeguards, and the CBDC stays outside credit creation and monetary-policy operations.
  Here we present a CBDC architecture based on grassroots currencies that overcomes these limitations. The architecture has three components: (1) Money: sovereign grassroots coins, which are digital debts of one unit of fiat currency issued by the central bank, constituting a direct CBDC; (2) Credit and Liquidity: non-sovereign grassroots coins, which are digital debts of one unit of the same fiat currency, redeemable at par, that can be issued by any person, natural or legal, thus adding credit; and (3) Interest: grassroots bonds, sovereign and non-sovereign, adding maturity and thus interest, standard banking instruments, and the central bank's instruments of monetary policy.
  The central bank can therefore lend, absorb liquidity, set its rates and buy and sell securities in the coins and bonds the public holds, choosing the counterparties and terms of its credit operations, and without converting bank deposits into newly issued central bank money on demand.
  We prove that the arbitrage-free price of any non-sovereign grassroots coin whose issuer redeems it on demand is one unit of the fiat currency. The central bank can choose to deal with any counterparty, not just banks, and we argue that the central bank's interest rates on lending and bonds bound from above and below the corresponding interest rates of its counterparties. Sovereign and non-sovereign grassroots coins and bonds have been implemented and tested on a small scale.
